newsitem.title: CHINA: Cuddly Communist to Beijing Butcher.
newsitem.headline: Cuddly Communist to Beijing Butcher.

text.p: He will be remembered for his catchy soundbites -- "to get rich is glorious" and "poverty is not socialism" -- his gravelly chain-smoker voice and a tiny frame that disguised a huge appetite for work and battle.
A soldier, statesman, politician and administrator, Deng Xiaoping stamped his mark on China like no other 20th century Chinese figure barring Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai.

Part of the famous Long March, an epic slog across China in 1934-35 to save a fledgling Communist movement from annhilation by the Chinese Nationalist government, Deng's signal contributions to his nation's history arguably came after his rise to supreme power in 1978.

Back in power after Mao's ultra-leftist Cultural Revolution from 1966-76, Deng began ripping apart Mao's legacy of collectivsed agriculture based on the communes. Peasants were encouraged to till their own land for cash crops to sell in private markets, while delivering a set portion of output to the state under a "responsibility system". With the extra money, rural enterprises sprouted. Later, the system was modified to give managers of urban state enterprises greater autonomy from party control.

A trip to the United States in 1979 opened Deng's eyes to the dismal state of China's economy. His "Four Modernisations" -- of agriculture, industry, science and national defence -- wrenched China into the contemporary world. After the People's Liberation Army received a bloody nose in a 1979 border war with Vietnam, he set about turning a military trained to fight a protracted "people's war" into a professional fighting machine. One quarter of the army was demobilised.

Steeped in a view of his country's history shaped by humiliation at the hands of imperialist powers led by Britain, Deng determined to recover the British colony of Hong Kong. A pragmatist, he recognised that Hong Kong would have to retain its free-wheeling markets to survive and flourish. Under the "one country, two systems" formula, Hong Kong will be returned to China at midnight on June 30, but will retain its capitalist system for 50 years.

For almost three decades since the 1949 communist revolution, China turned its back on the world. Deng flung open the doors to foreign investment and tourists, while fighting a rearguard action to prevent "flies and mosquitos" -- Western ideas of democracy and human rights -- from flitting in. He visited France, Japan, Southeast Asia and the United States, donning a 10-gallon cowboy hat to ride around a rodeo in a horse-drawn carriage.

In the eyes of the world, the cuddly communist became a butcher when he ordered troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy demonstrations around Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 4, 1989. Hundreds were killed on the spot and later thousands more were rounded up, put on trial and jailed or executed. For many people overseas and at home, the horrific images of China killing its own children were an indelible stain.

A family man, historians are not likely to uncover many personal skeletons in Deng's cupboard. Mao's political tyranny was matched by crude passions for young girls and drugs, according to posthumous accounts by his personal physician. Deng was rarely seen in public without one of his children or grandchildren. Not that Deng was without coarse peasant ways. He repelled former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, loudly expectorating in her presence in Beijing and making copious use of a spittoon. Former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger famously called him "a nasty little man".

Deng fearlessly challenged those in the party who sought to stunt China's economic growth by imposing political dogma and orthodoxy. In 1961 he first used the phrase, "It doesn't matter if the cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice".
